definition: Floating-point operations, the currency of compute.
details: Floating-point operations, the currency of compute. Training cost is estimated as ~6 x parameters x tokens FLOPs; regulation now even defines model tiers by training FLOPs. Comparing FLOPs to hardware peak throughput yields training-time estimates.

explainer.lead: FLOPs count the floating-point arithmetic needed to train or run an AI model. They turn model size and training data into a rough compute budget, helping teams estimate cost, time, and hardware needs.

tiers.eli5: Think of training an AI as doing an enormous pile of tiny maths problems. FLOPs tell you roughly how many problems are in the pile, while a computer's speed tells you how quickly it can work through them. This helps estimate whether training will take hours, days, or much longer.
tiers.practitioner: For transformer training, estimate compute as roughly 6 times the parameter count times the training-token count. Divide that total by hardware peak throughput for an idealized training-time estimate, using accelerator specifications to compare setups. Real runs take longer because peak throughput is not sustained throughput.
tiers.paperLevel: For N parameters and D training tokens, training compute is commonly approximated as C ≈ 6ND FLOPs. An idealized time estimate is T ≈ C/P_peak, where P_peak is hardware peak throughput in FLOP/s. These are approximations: FLOPs alone do not determine achieved throughput or wall-clock training time.

explainer.example: A 1-billion-parameter model trained on 10 billion tokens requires approximately 6 × 10^9 × 10^10 = 6 × 10^19 FLOPs. At a sustained 10^15 FLOP/s, that arithmetic would take about 60,000 seconds, or 16.7 hours; using only peak hardware throughput makes this an idealized estimate.

usedIn.name: LLM training planning
usedIn.detail: Estimates compute from a model's parameter count and training-token budget.

usedIn.name: AI hardware selection
usedIn.detail: Compares estimated training work with accelerator peak throughput.

usedIn.name: AI regulation
usedIn.detail: Training-FLOP thresholds can be used to define model tiers.

explainer.intuition: FLOPs are a way to count mathematical work rather than measure elapsed time. A bigger model or a larger token budget means more work, and hardware throughput determines how quickly that work could ideally be completed.
howItWorks: Count the tokens used for training.
Estimate training compute as 6 × parameters × tokens.
Divide by hardware peak throughput for an idealized time estimate.
explainer.whyItMatters: A common compute unit makes training plans and hardware options easier to compare before committing resources. Training-FLOP totals also provide a measurable basis for regulatory model tiers.
misconceptions: FLOPs count operations; FLOP/s measures operations per second.
A FLOP estimate is not a guarantee of training time.
Peak hardware throughput is not necessarily achieved in practice.
